claims.text: Conventional W–Cu composites have tungsten–copper interfaces with relatively high interfacial thermal resistance.
Applying a nanoscale Ag coating to tungsten particles before consolidation will reduce interfacial thermal resistance between tungsten and copper.
The Ag coating will produce an improved, well-bonded W–Ag–Cu interface.
The Ag interlayer enhances electron and phonon coupling across the W/Cu interface.
The Ag interlayer reduces carrier scattering at the W/Cu interface.
Enhanced coupling and reduced interfacial scattering lower thermal boundary resistance.
Silver has inherently high thermal conductivity.
Silver is compatible with both tungsten and copper.
Ag compatibility with tungsten and copper supports mechanical bond integrity.
Under suitably designed processing conditions, the Ag-containing interface is expected to retain performance under irradiation.
The Ag-coated composite will have approximately 10–20% higher effective thermal conductivity than the uncoated baseline.
The Ag-coated composite will maintain mechanical durability comparable to the uncoated baseline.
The Ag-coated composite will maintain irradiation resistance comparable to the uncoated baseline.
Vacuum or inert-atmosphere spark plasma sintering will ensure high densification of the Ag-coated W–Cu composite.
The uncoated W–Cu baseline has acceptable mechanical and irradiation properties.
Excessive Ag diffusion or brittle-phase formation during sintering or irradiation could negate the proposed benefit.
Defects introduced by the Ag-coating process could compromise mechanical integrity.

contradictions.description: The treated material is specified as consolidated by SPS, whereas the baseline is described as made by standard or conventional powder metallurgy; the experiment nevertheless says processing conditions will be identical aside from the coating. Unless both groups use the same SPS cycle, processing route and coating are confounded.
